Centipede behavior and husbandry, specifically in the genus Scolopendra. I have kept many different species of Scolopendra, namely S. subspinipes, S. morsitans, S. polymorpha, and S. alterans. This went on for years, over five, and although I currently have none in my collection, I hope to acquire more soon. I feel like this is the ultimate in useless knowledge, but there is something about their attitude, speed, and overall look that is fascinating to me.

That's really cool. Connecting to nature in such a deep way is awesome! It sounds like they influence you a bit :) out of all your Scolopendra, which was your absolute favorite? Or, if you don't have favorites, which one did you have for the longest extent of your time?

There was a particular Subspinipes that I had, which came from a friend that originally purchased it as wild caught, so I have no idea how old the thing was at the time. This one was definitely the most interesting, due to the fact that it was the absolute largest and ill-tempered in the collection. I think she was around 7 inches. She went absolutely wild over everything, and watching her hunt was astounding; centipedes will wander around and sort of bob their upper body up and down while their antennae probe around, and that movement is really mesmerizing and interesting -- she would spend hours doing it. Also, I have snakes and she would eat the frozen/thawed mice if my snakes refused food that day, which was nice because they usually go to waste when that happens. This became really long but I miss that little beastie.
Wow, she sounds fascinating. Did you encounter a lot of other people with an interest in these?

Not really, no. But I hung around with the local herpetological society, and some of those guys were in to invertebrates, but they were usually more in to animals that aren't venomous, so I was lonely in my centipede love. The person that gave me the aforementioned centipede was curious about getting one, but quickly realized that it wasn't something he liked.

Dirty secrets of the food manufacturing industry, including frozen foods, water bottling, and bioremediation. I know the legal loop holes (FDA, ISO, EPA, FSSC, IBWA, NELAC, TCEQ, a lot of food safety regulatory compliance). I know what corporations do to remain in business yet continue to break the law.

I'm a food industry insider for a very large food manufacturer.
Oh man, have anything really terrible to share with us?

Well for example, the fda requires all food manufacturers to list all the ingredients that go into a food product in its label. Food manufacturers have spent good money on lawyers to deconstruct and reinterpret the fine print and found a way out. They add harmful chemicals to extend shelf life of their products into the packaging prior to dispensing their foods into said packaging. By preemptively lacing the packaging with harmful chemicals, they can legally claim that no harmful chemicals are added to the food products... and this is because the hazardous chemical was "already there" inside the packaging before adding the food items. And by 'already there' I mean fractions of a second prior to filling or dispensing. This way they are exempt from disclosing all the chemicals found in their products. Adding hazardous chemicals to "food meant for human consumption" is not allowed, but adding food to hazardous chemicals is technically permissible. You can thank your congressmen for that. You would be surprised at the types and number of chemicals added to the inner lining of food products prior to dispensing or filling. Chemicals like carcinogens, sterilants, harmful preservatives, etc.
